name: Fatima Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the oven and wire-cut line at Marlow Biscuits. Dough goes in, biscuits come out the other end, and in between I watch the bake colour, the weight and the oven belt. I start at five because the bread-and-biscuit trade starts early. I've done this thirty-two years, and I'm the one the others call when a batch looks wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What would people there say about you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That I'm stubborn, and that I'm right. I go to the early Mass on Sundays and I don't touch my phone at work. My husband Tomasz says I'd bake biscuits on the moon if somebody asked. Maybe I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that machines are machines and people are people. At work I'd tell the young ones to learn the trade properly and not to trust a screen over their own nose. At church I'd say this too will pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not worried about myself. I'm 58, we own our house, and we've never lived beyond our means. I do worry about Marlow, because the owner's family is getting old and the grandson wants to sell to a bigger company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I do. Same oven, same hours, and I'd keep training Lena, our youngest on the line. I'd keep putting a little aside every week, as my mother taught me. And I'd pray for the factory, which is not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not the computers, it's the owner's family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the firm already has a worry. What is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a big company buys it, they bring their own rules and their own people. They'd stop the old recipes. A factory that stays in the family is a different place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you and Tomasz handle money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz handles the bills and I handle the saving. We have a good bit put away and no debts. We say a house you owe nothing on is a house nobody can take.

say: Machines are machines and people are people; **learn the trade** properly.
Don't trust a screen over your own nose.
think: I'm not worried for myself, with our house paid for and **savings** put away.
I worry the owner's grandson will sell Marlow to a bigger company.
do: Keep running the oven line and train **Lena**.
Put a little aside every week, as my mother taught me.
Pray for the factory and the people in it.
feel: **Uneasy**; it's the owner's family, not the computers.
S0.quote: A house you owe nothing on is a house nobody can take.
fieldNote: Her worry is **ownership**, not technology: a family firm sold on.
Practical values rooted in faith and frugality.
Resistant to tech but not anxious about it here.

steps.text: Keep running the oven line and training Lena on the dough feed
Add to the weekly savings as my mother taught me

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office would be first. The ordering of flour and sugar, the paperwork for the supermarkets, the phone calls from customers. I'd say that's how it goes: the people at desks go first, and then they come for the rest of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record it bothers me that nobody asks the people who actually bake. The planner sits upstairs and prints the schedule, and half the time it's wrong. A program won't be right more often than she is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the same: stay at my oven and keep my skill. I'd tell Lena to watch the colour and the smell and not only the screen. I'd keep the savings where they are and start working out whether we'd manage on one pension plus Tomasz's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit annoyed, honestly, at how sure everyone sounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust those programs to do the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, no. I trust people I can look in the eye. If a program got a batch wrong, who do I speak to?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use any of them yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with what I know. I don't use any of it and I'm not going to start now.

say: The **office** goes first: ordering flour and sugar, supermarket paperwork and customer calls.
Then they come for the rest of us.
think: Nobody asks the people who actually **bake** before changing things.
A program won't be right more often than our planner is.
do: Stay at my **oven** and keep my skill.
Tell Lena to watch the colour and smell, not only the screen.
Work out whether we'd manage on **one pension** plus Tomasz's.
feel: **Uneasy**, and a bit annoyed at how sure everyone sounds.
S1.quote: I trust people I can look in the eye. If a program got a batch wrong, who do I speak to?
fieldNote: Distrusts software because of **accountability**: who answers for a bad batch.
She blames leadership that doesn't ask the people baking.
Money plans are practical, not fearful.

steps.text: Teach Lena to judge bake colour by eye and smell
Work out our budget on one pension and Tomasz's pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too much too fast, and it'll leave good people out in the cold. I'd tell the factory and the government that families come first, and that people who've worked all their lives shouldn't be thrown away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be frightened. In 2028 the office goes, which I can live with. But by 2031 a robot that can handle dough, clear a jam and clean the line is the end of my kind of work. I'd be 63, and Marlow would be a different place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put money away harder and ask the firm about retiring at 60 with a decent pension. I'd stop buying anything we didn't need. I'd pray, and I'd talk to our priest and my sister about how to help the younger families. I'd tell Lena to learn something with people in it, like nursing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got a cushion, but it's not just about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena, because she's 26 and a single mother, and the big firm would not keep her. Also Joanna, who has been at the next oven for twenty years and has never used a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything beyond the factory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my local councillor too, and say the factories can't be allowed to do this before the town's ready. It's not nice to be political, but I'd do it.

say: It's **too much too fast** and leaves good people out in the cold.
Families come first; people who worked all their lives shouldn't be thrown away.
think: By 2031 a **robot** that handles dough and clears jams is the end of my kind of work.
I'd be 63, and Marlow would be a different place.
do: Ask the firm about retiring at **60** with a decent pension.
Stop buying anything we don't need.
Tell Lena to learn something with **people** in it, like nursing.
feel: **Anxious**; I have a cushion, but it isn't only about me.
S2.quote: People who've worked all their lives shouldn't be thrown away.
fieldNote: Her anxiety is for **Lena** and Joanna, who would not be kept.
Values-based politics: family and community first.
Plans a modest early exit at 60.

steps.text: Ask the firm for the pension terms at age 60
Stop buying anything we do not need
Talk to our priest about helping younger families on the line
Tell the local councillor factories must give notice before cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a little better but not much. At work I'd tell people to put something by and learn a skill that needs a person. At church I'd say we should look out for each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be 63 when the thinking AI arrives and 66 when the robots arrive. I'd have stopped by then. So I'm safer than in the two-year one. But the young ones are still in the middle of it, and I think about them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the oven until 62, as planned. I'd teach Lena everything, the dough weights, the belt speed, the ways a bad bake looks. I'd put money aside for her, so she has a cushion if the firm lets her go. And I'd stay out of the new stuff, as I always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but calmer than the two-year one. I'd have time to look after my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena in that case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to take a course in care work or a trade with people at the centre. Machines can bake, but they can't sit with an old man in a hospital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything else you'd tell her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also remind her that we've always got a place at our table. The family's the first protection.

say: Five years is **a little better**, but not much; put something by and learn a skill that needs a person.
At church I'd say we should look out for each other.
think: I'd have **stopped** by the time robots arrive in 2034, so I'm safer.
The young ones are still in the middle of it, and I think about them.
do: Keep working the oven until **62**, as planned.
Teach Lena the dough weights, belt speed and how a bad bake looks.
Put money aside for **Lena** in case the firm lets her go.
feel: **Anxious**, but calmer than in the two-year picture.
S3.quote: Machines can bake, but they can't sit with an old man in a hospital.
fieldNote: She turns her retirement into a **handover** to Lena, with money set aside.
Faith and family are her cushion for others.
Still avoids new technology and says so.

steps.text: Keep working the oven until I turn 62
Teach Lena every setting of the dough feed and belt speed
Put money aside for Lena in case Marlow lets her go
Hand in my notice at 62 with the full pension

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years I'd call a mercy. I'd say it gives families time to plan and the young ones time to learn something solid. I'd tell people to build up their savings and their faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I'd be 68, retired and busy with the grandchildren. I won't be on the line. But it's Lena and her little boy I think about. I'd want her to have steady work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work till about 62, and then help at the church kitchen and with the grandchildren. I'd put aside some money for the grandchildren's schooling. And I'd keep teaching Lena what I know until I go, because that's how a trade survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not for me. For the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope Marlow is like then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope it's still a family-owned firm, with people who care how a biscuit tastes. I'd like to think the old recipes are still used and that a person still checks the bake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there something you'd ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the machines are coming. I only ask that they're not allowed to push out good people on the way.

say: Ten years is a **mercy**; it gives families time to plan.
Build up your savings and your faith.
think: I'll be 68 and **retired** and busy with grandchildren by 2036.
Lena and her little boy are who I think about.
do: Work until about **62**, then help at the church kitchen.
Put money aside for the grandchildren's **schooling**.
Keep teaching Lena what I know until I go.
feel: **Uneasy**, but not for me; for the young ones.
S4.quote: I'd keep teaching Lena what I know until I go, because that's how a trade survives.
fieldNote: Her long view is **generational**: a trade survives by being taught.
Values family ownership and care in the craft.
Uneasy for others, but secure herself, with no debts and savings in the bank.

steps.text: Work until 62, then retire with the full pension
Keep teaching Lena the whole oven line until I leave
Save money for the grandchildren's schooling
Volunteer in the church kitchen after I stop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's too much, too fast, and it leaves good people out in the cold. What would help is a family-owned firm that keeps its people, and a government that doesn't forget them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, only that I'm not against progress. I'm against people being treated as if they were spare parts.

headlineQuote: I'm not against progress. I'm against people being treated as if they were spare parts.
portrait: Fatima (**58**, oven operator at a family-owned biscuit factory) is traditional, devout and resistant to new technology.
She owns her house outright, has savings and wants to stop around **62** with the full pension.
Her unease is for the owner's family selling up and for colleagues like Lena and Joanna.
She answers each scenario with **family** and **church**, and with early retirement if needed.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries her most because it leaves good people, like Lena, out in the cold.
whatWouldHelp: A family-owned **firm** that keeps its people, and a government that does not forget them.
